l5_paragraph_proof.case_name: HKSAR v Mo Yuk Ping and Another
l5_paragraph_proof.exact_quote: a concealment attracts criminal liability only if it was made in breach of a duty of disclosure
l5_paragraph_proof.paragraph_text: 3. The Court held that in relation to the actus reus of a section 16A offence, under well-established common law principles, a concealment attracts criminal liability only if it was made in breach of a duty of disclosure. To secure a conviction, the prosecution had to prove beyond reasonable doubt that: (1) Dico Consultants’ occupation and use of the Premises constituted a breach of the leasing instruments. (2) Apple Daily Printing, as the contracting party, was under a duty to disclose the breach to the Corporation under the leasing instruments. (3) Apple Daily Printing’s duty of disclosure was attributable to the applicants, so that their failure to disclose the breach to the Corporation constituted a concealment under section 16A. (4) Alternatively, the applicants were under an independent personal duty to disclose the breach to the Corporation. (5) Further or alternatively, the applicants made a false representation to the Corporation that the Premises had been used for the Specified Purpose.

l5_paragraph_proof.case_name: HKSAR v Mo Yuk Ping and Another
l5_paragraph_proof.exact_quote: no general duty to disclose one’s own breach of contract
l5_paragraph_proof.paragraph_text: 4. Applying well-established case law to the facts, the Court held that: (1) Dico Consultant’s occupation and use of the Premises constituted a breach of the leasing instruments. (2) In relation to concealment: (a) Under the common law, there is no general duty to disclose one’s own breach of contract. A lease does not generally fall within any established category of contracts where such a duty of disclosure is imposed. (b) In arguing that there was such a duty of disclosure imposed on Apple Daily Printing, the prosecution relied on express terms or alternatively implied terms of the leasing instruments; and the special nature of the instruments that gave rise to a special relationship between the parties. (c) However, the leasing instruments contained no such express term or, on a proper construction, such an implied term. (d) On the parties’ relationship, while the leasing instruments contained some special features, what existed between the parties was essentially a commercial landlord-tenant relationship: (i) As required by statute, the Corporation must act in accordance with prudent commercial principles. From its perspective, the relationship with the lessee was commercial in nature. So was the case from the lessee’s perspective. (ii) The preferential rates and tenure granted by the Corporation are important attractions to the lessee. However, the lessee has to satisfy the Corporation with the merits of its proposed projects in order to gain approval for admission to the Estate. One of the considerations taken into account by the Corporation was the size of investment proposed by the lessee. In the present case, Apple Daily Printing had invested HK$528 million into the construction of the Premises. Balancing the costs incurred and the benefits involved, including the preferential rates and tenure, to determine if the project was viable clearly entailed a careful commercial decision on Apple Daily Printing’s part. (iii) The Corporation’s decision to grant the lease to Apple Daily Printing was also a careful commercial decision ensuring that the grant of preferential rates and tenure was justified. (iv) Apple Daily Printing did not stand alone to benefit in terms of preferential rates and tenure. The Corporation would also benefit from the improvement in the land value from the construction of the Premises. Further, the Corporation must have been satisfied that Apple Daily Printing’s undertakings would facilitate the overall development of Hong Kong’s economy by broadening its industrial base and upgrading technology levels, which are substantial benefits that the Corporation, tasked by the Government to promote Hong Kong’s industry and technology, would stand to gain. (e) Accordingly, what existed between Apple Daily Printing and the Corporation was not a special relationship which constituted an exception to the common law rule that no duty of disclosure of breach arises in the performance of an already concluded contract. (f) Noting that the leasing instruments appeared to be standard contracts, the Court observed that if the prosecution were right on the duty of disclosure, it might potentially apply to all tenants in the Estate. The Court had reservations if such a sweeping proposition truly represented the Corporation’s leasing policy or contractual intent. (g) Even if Apple Daily Printing was under such a duty of disclosure, it could not as a matter of law be attributed to the applicants: (i) The prosecution did not rely on section 101E of the Criminal Procedure Ordinance, which is the most obvious route. (ii) The prosecution instead relied on the common law rule that corporate bodies are deemed to act and acquire knowledge through those individuals who are its directing mind. However, that rule attributes criminal liability to a company through the acts or omissions of its directing mind. It does not operate in an opposite way of attributing the company’s criminal liability to its officers. (h) The prosecution had not advanced any substantial submission why the applicants were under an independent personal duty of disclosure to the Corporation. (3) On the available evidence, the prosecution failed to prove beyond reasonable doubt that the applicants had made the false representation that the Premises had been used for the Specified Purpose. (4) The Court therefore concluded that the prosecution had failed to prove the applicants had committed the actus reus of the fraud charges. (5) For completeness, in relation to mens rea , the Court observed that the trial judge had failed to consider certain important matters that were relevant to the applicants’ state of mind.

l5_paragraph_proof.case_name: Betty Kwan and Others v Securities and Futures Commission
l5_paragraph_proof.exact_quote: S 300 is a general provision that outlaws fraudulent conduct in securities transactions
l5_paragraph_proof.paragraph_text: 9. The Court held that the word “transaction” should be interpreted by the context and purpose of s 300. S 300 is a general provision that outlaws fraudulent conduct in securities transactions. Adopting this approach, the word “transaction”, for the purpose of s 300, must be given a wide meaning.

l5_paragraph_proof.case_name: Betty Kwan and Others v Securities and Futures Commission
l5_paragraph_proof.exact_quote: insider dealing is a species of fraud
l5_paragraph_proof.paragraph_text: 12. Moreover, insider dealing is a species of fraud. It is a fraud on the public and not a victimless crime. Since it is undisputed that the appellants would have contravened s 291(5) of the SFO for inside dealing but for the fact that Hsinchu Bank shares were not listed in Hong Kong, their conduct amounted to a species of fraud which comes within s 300. Given that substantial activities constituting the complaint under s 300 occurred in Hong Kong, the appellants’ conduct is covered by s 300. CONCLUSION:
